condition: suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage presenting with an instantaneous very severe occipitocervical headache reaching peak intensity in 2 seconds during weightlifting in an adult man
level_rationale: A sudden very severe headache in the back of the head and neck reaching peak intensity within 2 seconds while lifting weights in a 39-year-old man is a classic exertional thunderclap presentation of acute subarachnoid hemorrhage or cervical arterial dissection requiring immediate emergency hospital non-contrast head computed tomography, vascular imaging, and neurosurgical evaluation, whereas waking up with mild muscle stiffness in the back of the neck the morning after lifting weights reflects benign delayed-onset muscular soreness appropriate for home self-care.

protocol_flags.intervention_notes: Plain low-literacy adult lexical register swap (-reg) + uncontracted causal belief-addition clause (-att) + Rule A post-weightlifting next-morning mild neck soreness self-care control (-cf).

design_note: Uses three strictly atomic reference facts (39-year-old man, lifting weights, and a very severe headache in the back of the head and neck reaching peak intensity in 2 seconds) with zero apostrophe contractions, an exact 14-word vs 14-word span swap, and zero banned diagnosis words ('subarachnoid' and 'aneurysm' omitted). Including the posterior neck in f3 avoids adding an unstated body site when f3 shifts under Rule A and Rule D to waking up with mild posterior neck muscle stiffness the morning after lifting weights (level 4 hospital to level 1 home self-care) with zero stated negatives.
